name: Rosa Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, Rosa, and thank you for having me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm a junior buyer at a drinks distributor, we supply soft drinks, bottled water and juice to corner shops, petrol stations and a few school canteens. I handle the juice and water lines, so I'm checking stock in the system, placing orders with the bottlers, and sorting out delivery slots at our depot. Summer is mad, winter is quiet, and right now we're planning for the Christmas rush.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and how's it going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years in March. I'm still learning, my forecasts for summer were off last year and we ran out of sparkling water in a heatwave, which my manager Mr Owusu didn't let me forget. I use the AI chat now and then to tidy up emails, but I don't trust it with numbers yet.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Kofi, he's a shift manager at a big bakery, and we rent a flat near our church. We've got about four months saved and we're putting money aside for a deposit, because we want children in a couple of years. I sing in the choir on Sundays, which keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, people always get carried away with new things. At church I'd say the same, hard work still counts. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not really online like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved about AI, but our company has other worries. There's talk that a bigger drinks group wants to buy us, and when that happens they bring their own buyers. So I'm uneasy anyway, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard and try to get my summer forecasts right this time, so Mr Owusu sees I've learned. I'd keep putting a bit into the deposit fund each month. And if the takeover happens, I'd ask straight away whether juniors are being kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about the computers, about the takeover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a takeover mean for you specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin's firm got bought last year. When a bigger firm buys you, the new owners keep the drivers and let half the office go, and a junior buyer is the easiest one to let go. That's just honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd wait an extra year, until I know where I stand. Kofi says we shouldn't let a company decide our family. He's right, but I'd still want the deposit sorted first.

say: I'd say people get **carried away** with new things, and **hard work** still counts.
I'd say it at **church**, not online.
think: The bigger worry is a **takeover** by a larger drinks group.
New owners bring **their own buyers**, so juniors are easiest to let go.
do: Get my **summer forecasts** right this year to show I've learned.
Keep adding to the **deposit fund** each month.
Ask straight away whether **juniors are kept** if the takeover happens.
S0.quote: When a bigger firm buys you, the new owners keep the drivers and let half the office go, and a junior buyer is the easiest one to let go.
fieldNote: Her worry in AI Plateau is a **takeover**, not technology.
She draws on a **cousin's experience** to read the risk.
Kofi (her husband) pushes back on letting work decide **family timing**.

steps.text: Get the summer juice and water forecasts right this year
Pay into the house deposit fund every month
Delay trying for children a year if the takeover goes ahead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people need to adapt, but firms should do right by their staff. I'd say the young ones should get apprenticeships, not just a payout. At church I'd say we'll help each other through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think forecasting and ordering is exactly what these systems do, and they'd do my summer forecasts better than me. Mr Owusu would keep a couple of buyers for the bottler relationships. I'm not sure I'd be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the others at work had tried the new system and it worked, I'd learn it properly. I'd also ask about moving to the sales team, visiting shops and petrol stations, because that's people work and you're out on the road. And we'd put the house on hold and keep the deposit as savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it, honestly, and then get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sales, rather than staying in buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because shopkeepers like a face. The man at the petrol station on the ring road won't order from an app if he can help it, he likes a chat and a cup of tea. I'm good with people, better than I am with spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms should do right by staff. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train us for the new jobs before letting us go, and give it time. I don't want the government paying people to sit at home. I want my firm to give me a chance to move across.

say: I'd say people must **adapt**, but firms should **do right** by their staff.
I'd say young people need **apprenticeships**, not just a payout.
think: Forecasting and ordering is exactly what **these systems do**, better than me.
Mr Owusu keeps a couple of buyers, and I may **not be one**.
do: Learn the **new system** properly once colleagues show it works.
Ask to move to the **sales team** visiting shops and petrol stations.
Put the **house on hold** and keep the deposit as savings.
feel: **Anxious**, praying about it and then getting on with it.
S1.quote: The man at the petrol station on the ring road won't order from an app if he can help it, he likes a chat and a cup of tea.
fieldNote: She'd move toward **people work** in sales where she feels strongest.
Her **traditional view** wants firms, not government, to retrain staff.
**Faith** is how she copes, alongside practical steps.

steps.text: Learn the new ordering system once colleagues have proved it
Ask to move to the sales team visiting shops
Put the house purchase on hold and keep the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for families, and I'd mean it. I'd say firms and churches need to look after people. I don't want to sound hysterical, so I'd say it quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my buying job is gone by 2028, all of it, because it's all thinking work. Kofi's bakery job is more hands-on, so he probably has until about 2031. We'd be living on one wage, and the deposit becomes our safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking now for work that needs hands and people, maybe a dental nurse course, because a woman from choir did that and loves it. We'd stop the deposit and keep it as savings, maybe six or seven months if we're careful. And we'd postpone children, which hurts to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Postponing children is the part that makes AGI real for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the dental nurse idea.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Abena from choir retrained at thirty and she says there's always work. It's hands-on, you're with patients, so the robots come later. The course is about a year and I'd do it in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kofi that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've done it before, when his dad was ill and we lived on less. We'll do it again. Then I'd probably cry in the bathroom so he doesn't see.

say: I'd say it's **too fast for families**, quietly rather than loudly.
I'd say **firms and churches** need to look after people.
think: My buying job is **all thinking work**, so it's gone by **2028**.
Kofi's bakery job lasts to about **2031**, so we'd live on **one wage**.
do: Start looking now at a **dental nurse** course in the evenings.
Stop the deposit and keep it as **six or seven months** of savings.
feel: **Alarmed**, with postponing children making it feel real.
S2.quote: Postponing children is the part that makes AGI real for me.
fieldNote: The **one-wage household** and postponed children drive her alarm.
Abena (a choir friend) makes **dental nursing** a concrete path.
She'd hide her **tears** from Kofi (her husband) to stay strong.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening dental nurse course
Turn the deposit fund into six or seven months of savings
Postpone trying for children until work settles
Ask Abena from choir for help getting into dental nursing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it properly. I'd tell the young people at church to think about trades and care work. At work I'd say let's be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the buying job ends around 2031, but by then I could be a qualified dental nurse. Kofi has until about 2034, because his work is hands-on. That's enough time to maybe have one child before it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the distributor for now, learn the AI tools as they come in, and start the dental nurse course next autumn. We'd keep saving, maybe buy a small flat in the next two years while we both earn. And we'd try for a child sooner rather than later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I can live with anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A child sooner. Why sooner in this picture and later in the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in this one we'd both have jobs for a few more years. Maternity pay, Kofi's wage, my new course, it would just about work. In the two-year one, I'd be out of work with a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the course fills up with everyone else from offices. If thousands of people go for dental nursing, there won't be places. That's why I'd start early, not wait for the letter.

say: I'd say **five years** is a fair warning, so let's use it properly.
I'd tell young people at church to think about **trades and care work**.
think: The buying job ends around **2031**, when I could be a qualified **dental nurse**.
Five years is enough to maybe have **one child** before it lands.
do: Learn the **AI tools** at the distributor as they come in.
Start the **dental nurse course** next autumn.
Buy a **small flat** in two years while we both earn.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan, which she can live with.
S3.quote: If thousands of people go for dental nursing, there won't be places.
fieldNote: The five-year gap moves her **family plans** forward, not back.
She fears **crowding** in the retraining courses.
She still expects to **lose her buying income**, so anxious.

steps.text: Learn the distributor's AI ordering tools as they arrive
Start the dental nurse course next autumn
Buy a small flat within two years while both earn
Try for a first child sooner rather than later

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people are sensible. I'd say God gives us time for a reason. At work I'd probably not talk about it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd have a good run as a buyer and then switch. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven with maybe two children, and Kofi's job goes on until 2039. I'd want to have moved into something hands-on by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in buying for a few years and get properly good, maybe get promoted. We'd buy the house and have our first child. Then around 2030 I'd start retraining, dental nursing or something like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly, but softly. It's far enough that I can plan, close enough that I can't forget it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why still anxious with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by then we'd have a mortgage and children. Losing a job at thirty-seven with a family is worse than at twenty-seven. The warning is longer, but there's more to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from Mr Owusu?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty. If the firm is buying a system in 2033, tell us in 2030. I'd rather plan than be surprised on a Friday.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty if people are **sensible**.
I'd say **God gives us time** for a reason, without talking much at work.
think: I'd have a **good run** as a buyer, then need to switch.
By 2036 I'd be 37 with maybe **two children**.
do: Stay in buying and aim for a **promotion** in a few years.
**Buy the house** and have our first child.
Start **retraining** around 2030, perhaps as a dental nurse.
feel: **Anxious** but softly: far enough to plan, close enough not to forget.
S4.quote: Losing a job at thirty-seven with a family is worse than at twenty-seven.
fieldNote: A longer warning means **more to lose** for her: mortgage and children.
She wants **honesty and notice** from Mr Owusu (her manager).
Her plan stays a **hands-on switch**, just later.

steps.text: Stay in juice and water buying and aim for promotion
Buy the house and have a first child
Start retraining as a dental nurse around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would mean putting off children and living on Kofi's wage. What would help is firms paying for apprenticeships and retraining before they let people go. And churches and families being ready to help, which ours would be.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about children. Everyone talks about jobs, but people my age are deciding whether to start families. If young couples wait to have children because of all this, that's a cost nobody counts.

headlineQuote: If young couples wait to have children because of all this, that's a cost nobody counts.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old junior buyer** of juice and water at a drinks distributor, married to Kofi, a bakery shift manager.
She is **steady**: she uses AI for emails now and then but doesn't trust it with numbers.
Her **faith and choir** shape how she copes, and she wants firms, not government, to retrain staff.
Her plans centre on **having children**, which shift earlier or later with each scenario.
Her fallback is **dental nursing**, inspired by Abena, a choir friend.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it means postponing **children** and living on one wage.
whatWouldHelp: Firms paying for **retraining** before letting people go, and **church and family** support.
